title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
directAnswer: The minimum of a rotated sorted array is the unique 'pivot' — the only element smaller than its predecessor. Binary search by comparing nums[mid] to nums[hi]: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum is strictly to the right (lo = mid + 1); otherwise it's at mid or to its left (hi = mid). Loop while lo < hi and return nums[lo]. O(log n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Binary search for the pivot via mid-vs-hi
remember.formula:
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo < hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid
return nums[lo]
rules: Compare `nums[mid]` to `nums[hi]`, **not** `nums[lo]` — comparing to lo is ambiguous when the array isn't rotated.
`nums[mid] > nums[hi]` ⇒ the drop is to the right ⇒ `lo = mid + 1` (mid can't be the min).
Else ⇒ mid could be the min, so `hi = mid` (keep mid in the window — do **not** write `mid - 1`).
Loop condition is `while (lo < hi)` because `hi = mid` keeps the window non-empty; with `<=` plus `hi = mid` you'd loop forever.
When the loop ends `lo == hi` points at the minimum — return `nums[lo]`.
whenToUse: Find the smallest element / rotation count / pivot of a rotated sorted array in O(log n)
Locate the single discontinuity in an otherwise-sorted sequence
As a sub-routine before searching a rotated array by splitting it at the pivot
antiSignals: Array isn't rotated and you just want min of arbitrary data → linear scan is O(n) and unavoidable
Duplicates allowed (LeetCode 154) → nums[mid] == nums[hi] is ambiguous; shrink hi by one, worst case O(n)
You also need to *search* for a target → combine with Search in Rotated Sorted Array
remember.takeaway: Comparing the midpoint to the right end (not the left) is the clean way to detect which side the rotation 'drop' is on. The `hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`) move with a `lo < hi` loop is the canonical boundary-finding template — memorise the pairing.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can find a boundary (the rotation point) with binary search, choosing the right anchor to compare against and pairing `hi = mid` with `while (lo < hi)` correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing nums[mid] to nums[lo] (ambiguous on a non-rotated array), or writing `hi = mid - 1` with the `hi = mid` style and skipping the true minimum, or using `lo <= hi` and looping forever.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain that the minimum is the only element smaller than its neighbour, justify comparing to nums[hi], and note the loop invariant: the minimum is always inside [lo, hi].

problemStatement:
Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in ascending order is **rotated** between `1` and `n` times. Given the sorted rotated array `nums` of **unique** elements, return the **minimum element** of this array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique
nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times
understanding: A rotation moves a suffix of the sorted array to the front, creating exactly one place where a bigger value is followed by a smaller one. That smaller value is the global minimum (the pivot). We binary search for it without ever needing the target.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are elements unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes here. Duplicates (LeetCode 154) make nums[mid] == nums[hi] ambiguous and degrade the worst case to O(n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed to be rotated at least once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The statement says rotated between 1 and n times, and rotating n times returns the original — so a fully sorted array is a valid input and the code must handle it (it does: hi keeps moving left to index 0).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I compare mid to lo or to hi?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: To hi. Comparing to lo can't distinguish a rotated from a non-rotated left segment; comparing to hi cleanly tells you which side the drop is on.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Return the value or the index?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The value here. If you needed the rotation count, you'd return the index lo instead.

Initialising min to 0 instead of nums[0] — wrong for all-positive or all-negative arrays.

approaches.name: Binary Search for the Pivot (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'find the single drop point' and anchor the compare on nums[hi].
hints: The minimum is the only element smaller than the one before it. How can comparing the middle element to the LAST element tell you which side that drop is on?
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the right portion is 'lower' and must contain the drop, so the minimum is to the right of mid.
Otherwise mid is part of the run that leads down to hi, so the minimum is mid or to its left — keep mid in the window with hi = mid, and loop while lo < hi.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration discards half the window with O(1) work → O(log n) iterations, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain `[lo, hi]` and shrink it toward the pivot.

**Why compare against `nums[hi]`.** The right end `nums[hi]` is a reliable reference for 'which side is the rotation on'. If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, then going from `mid` to `hi` we must pass through the drop — so the minimum lies strictly to the **right** of `mid`, and we set `lo = mid + 1` (mid itself can't be the minimum because something to its right is smaller). If instead `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]`, the segment `[mid, hi]` is already sorted (no drop), so the minimum is at `mid` or to its **left**; we set `hi = mid`, deliberately keeping `mid` because it might *be* the answer. Comparing to `nums[lo]` instead fails on an un-rotated array, where `nums[mid] >= nums[lo]` would wrongly push us right.

**Why `hi = mid` and not `hi = mid - 1`.** When `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]`, mid is a *candidate* minimum, so excluding it could throw away the answer. Keeping it (`hi = mid`) is correct; progress is still guaranteed because the `lo = mid + 1` branch always shrinks, and in the `hi = mid` branch `mid < hi` whenever `lo < hi` (mid rounds down), so `hi` strictly decreases.

**Why `while (lo < hi)`.** With `hi = mid`, a window of size 1 (`lo == hi`) already pinpoints the minimum, so we stop there and return `nums[lo]`. Using `lo <= hi` together with `hi = mid` would never let the window reach size 0 and would loop forever when `lo == hi == mid`. This `lo < hi` + `hi = mid` pairing is the standard 'find leftmost element satisfying a predicate' template.

**Why no explicit equality check.** Elements are unique and we're not searching for a value, only the boundary, so there's no `nums[mid] == target` case — we converge purely by halving toward the drop.
approaches.insight: This is the boundary-finding form of binary search: we're locating the leftmost index whose value is `<= nums[hi]`, i.e. the start of the lower sorted run. Recognising 'find the first index where a monotone predicate flips' lets you reuse this exact `lo < hi` / `hi = mid` skeleton for Search Insert Position, Find Peak Element, and rotation-count problems.

pitfalls: Comparing nums[mid] to nums[lo] — fails on un-rotated arrays.
Writing hi = mid - 1 with this template — skips the actual minimum.
Using `while (lo <= hi)` with hi = mid — infinite loop when lo == hi == mid.
Returning nums[mid] inside the loop instead of nums[lo] after convergence.

commonMistakes: Anchoring the comparison on nums[lo] instead of nums[hi], which is ambiguous when the array isn't rotated.
Pairing hi = mid with a `lo <= hi` loop, causing an infinite loop.
Excluding mid via hi = mid - 1 and skipping the true minimum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to nums[lo] instead of nums[hi]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a non-rotated array nums[mid] >= nums[lo] is always true, so anchoring on lo wrongly pushes the search right and never finds the front-most minimum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: hi = mid - 1 drops the minimum
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When nums[mid] <= nums[hi], mid is itself a candidate for the minimum. Setting hi = mid - 1 can step over it and return the wrong element.
